title: Lumbar Referred Pain | Visceral Referred Pain
purpose: Screen low back pain for true visceral pain and visceral referred pain so that serious pathology can be ruled out or referred on; 90% of low back pain is non-specific, but visceral sources are often overlooked.
structure: Organs sharing segmental innervation with the lumbar spine: urogenital tract; parts of the digestive tract (most digestive organs refer to the thoracic spine); abdominal aortic aneurysm (cardiovascular, otherwise thoracic). Visceral pain is diffuse, midline, poorly localized because of sparse visceral innervation and central divergence, and often accompanied by autonomic signs (pallor, sweating, nausea, GI upset, temperature/blood pressure/heart rate changes) and strong affective responses (Sikandar et al. 2012).
procedure: History screening. Urogenital: pain/difficulty urinating, haematuria, incontinence, frequency, decreased stream, impotence, last period, vaginal discharge, postmenopausal bleeding, urinary infections, menstrual pain, painful intercourse, venereal disease. Digestive: dysphagia, nausea/heartburn/vomiting, food intolerances, constipation, diarrhoea, stool colour change, rectal bleeding. AAA warning signs: abdominal pulsation lying down, dull mid-abdominal/left flank/low back ache. Locomotor tract: insidious multi-joint pain/swelling/restriction (inflammatory disease). Start with general questions and explain why you ask.
positive: A pattern rather than a single answer: symptoms unrelated to position or movement and present at rest or waking the patient at night; diffuse dull cramping pain that builds and recedes; symptoms linked to eating, bowel/bladder fullness, urination or defecation; insidious onset without trauma; fever, chills, nausea, unexplained weight loss, malaise, vomiting, bowel changes or rectal/vaginal bleeding for more than 1-2 weeks; risk from age, sex, occupation, ethnicity, past and family history.
notes: The goal is not to diagnose organ pathology (a physician's task) but to make visceral screening routine and refer out. The organ overview lists on the page are images not present in the API text. Companion pages: thoracic and cervical referred pain.

title: Somatic & Visceral Referred Pain Explained | Pain Neurophysiology
purpose: Explain the neurophysiology of somatic and visceral referred pain and how it differs from local pain, neuropathic pain and radicular pain.
structure: Convergence-projection theory: sparsely innervated deep/axial/proximal tissues (ligaments, capsules, tendons, fascia, muscle, e.g. low back or hip) converge on the same dorsal-horn second-order neuron as densely innervated distal tissue; the somatosensory cortex makes a projection error toward the distal tissue. Somatic example: right L5/S1 facet joint felt in the right buttock and posterior thigh. Visceral: organ nociception felt in somatic structures with the same segmental innervation, often with autonomic phenomena.
procedure: n/a (concept page). Clues: local pain increases with pressure at the painful site; referred pain does not, but pressure on the sensitized source increases both local and referred pain. Referred pain is felt within the same sclerotome (maps inconsistent), always proximal to distal, deep aching/expanding pressure, rarely distal to the knee or elbow (unlike radicular pain).
notes: Deep aching quality = unmyelinated type IV/C fibres (secondary hyperalgesia); sharp well-localized pain = myelinated type III/A-delta fibres (primary hyperalgesia). Referral patterns indicate approximate segmental location, not the anatomical source. The organ-referral overview image is not in the API text; the text contains a leftover production note ('Display overview from different studies if possible').

title: Closed Fist Percussion Test | Thoracic Compression Fracture
purpose: Red-flag screening for symptomatic vertebral (osteoporotic) compression fractures in patients presenting with sudden back pain.
structure: Vertebral bodies; osteoporotic compression fractures are the most common spinal red flag (prevalence 25% in women over 65 and 40% over 80).
procedure: Patient stands in front of a mirror so the reaction can be seen; the examiner stands behind, places one hand on the spine and percusses along the spine with the closed fist of the other hand.
notes: Companion test: supine sign. Other fracture screens listed: Caradeniz wrist rules, elbow extension test, patellar-pubic percussion, fulcrum test, Ottawa knee and ankle rules.

title: Supine Sign | Thoracic Compression Fracture
purpose: Red-flag screening for symptomatic vertebral compression fractures.
structure: Vertebral bodies, mostly thoracic; lying supine increases compression there.
procedure: Ask the patient to lie supine on the bench with only one pillow.
positive: The patient is unable to lie supine because of severe pain. History often reveals sleeping in a chair.

title: Babinski Sign to Screen for Upper Motor Neuron Lesions
purpose: Screen for upper motor neuron (pyramidal tract) lesions.
procedure: Run a pointed object from the heel along the lateral border of the sole forward toward the great toe.
positive: Extension of the big toe with fanning (abduction) of the other toes (fan sign, signe de l'éventail); in severe cases with hip and knee flexion. Normal response: flexor/grasping of the toes. Indicates structural pyramidal damage or temporary disturbance (epilepsy, intoxication).
notes: Other UMN screens on the page: Hoffmann's sign, Lhermitte's sign, inverted supinator sign (cervical). SOURCE NOTE: the page writes 'signe de Levante' (correct term is signe de l'éventail) and its first reference is garbled (Jaramillo citation merged with an unrelated BPPV guideline).

title: Schober Test | Lumbar Spine Flexion | Spinal Mobility Assessment
purpose: Quantify lumbar spine flexion; the modified version is part of the BASMI index for ankylosing spondylitis.
structure: Lumbar spine; skin marks relative to S2.
procedure: Patient barefoot, upright, feet 30 cm apart. Mark 5 cm below the S2 spinous process and 10 cm above it (15 cm apart). The patient flexes forward as far as possible with knees straight; re-measure. The difference is the flexion range. Modified Schober uses the iliac crest level as landmark; the modified-modified version uses the PSIS.
positive: Not a positive/negative test: the increase in distance quantifies lumbar flexion.

accuracy.source: n/a; Castro et al. systematic review (cited as 2015 in text, 2016 in references) reports acceptable construct validity

notes: SOURCE NOTE: this page says the modified Schober uses the iliac crest, while the modified-modified Schober page says the 'original Schober' uses the iliac crest; the two pages are inconsistent.

title: Modified-modified Schober Test | Lumbar Spine Flexion
purpose: Clinic-friendly quantification of lumbar flexion range (BASMI context, ankylosing spondylitis).
structure: Lumbar spine; skin marks relative to the PSIS line.
procedure: Patient upright. Draw a horizontal line between the two PSIS and mark a second point 15 cm above it. The patient bends forward as far as possible with knees extended; re-measure the distance.
positive: Not a positive/negative test: the increase in distance quantifies flexion.

accuracy.source: n/a; Rezvani et al. 2012: intra-rater reliability r 0.97 (excellent), correlation with radiographic measurement r 0.67 (moderate)

notes: Page rates moderate clinical value. See source-inconsistency note on the Schober test record.

title: Menell Test | 3-Phase Test | Quick Back / SIJ / Hip Assessment
purpose: Quick three-phase test to judge whether pain originates from the hip, the sacroiliac joint or the lumbar spine.
structure: Hip joint (closed-packed in internal rotation and extension), sacroiliac joint, lumbar spine.
procedure: Patient prone. Phase 1 (hip): fixate the pelvis at the ischial tuberosity in a ventrocaudal direction, hold the ipsilateral leg from the inside to create internal rotation and extend the hip. Phase 2 (SIJ): fixate the sacrum below its S2 pivot point ventrocaudally and extend the leg again. Phase 3 (lumbar): fixate T12 ventrocaudally with a pinch grip and extend the leg, producing passive extension and rotation of the whole lumbar spine.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar pain in the respective phase.
notes: For region-specific follow-up the page points to the Cluster of Laslett and Cluster of van der Wurff (SIJ) and the FADDIR test (hip). No references listed.

title: Dermatomes Lower Limb | Peripheral Neurological Examination
purpose: Sensory (dermatome) testing in suspected lumbar radiculopathy to help identify the pathological disc level.
structure: Lumbosacral dermatomes; nerve root compromise is most common at L4/L5 and L5/S1, far less at L3/L4 and rarely above.
procedure: Patient supine with the lower limbs exposed. Stroke the dermatome regions with a brush (e.g. from the reflex hammer handle) on affected and unaffected limbs and ask for side-to-side differences.
positive: Altered sensation within a dermatome compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: Al Nezari et al. 2013 systematic review/meta-analysis (14 studies, lumbar disc herniation); page spells 'Al Nazari'

notes: Weak clinical value (findings barely change post-test probability) but still the best physical-assessment tool. Companion pages: myotomes and reflexes lower limb (myotomes page is also in the knee module).

title: Myotomes Lower Limb | Peripheral Neurological Examination
purpose: Myotome strength testing of the lower limb to help identify the pathological disc level in suspected lumbar radiculopathy.
structure: Lumbosacral nerve roots: L2 hip flexion, L3 hip extension (as listed on the page), L4 tibialis anterior/ankle dorsiflexion, L5 extensor hallucis longus/great toe extension, S1 calf (repeated calf raises), S2 knee flexion (root pathology rare).
procedure: Patient supine; test each myotome and compare the affected with the unaffected side.
positive: Weakness (paresis) within a myotome compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: Al Nezari et al. 2013 systematic review/meta-analysis, 14 studies, lumbar disc herniation

notes: Same page is also included in the knee module. Positive or negative findings barely change post-test probability (weak clinical value), yet it remains the best physical-assessment tool available. SOURCE NOTE: the page lists L3 as hip extension without comment.

title: Lower Limb Reflex Testing | Peripheral Neurological Examination
purpose: Deep tendon reflex testing in suspected lumbar radiculopathy to help identify the pathological disc level.
structure: Patellar tendon reflex (L3-L4) and Achilles tendon reflex (L5-S1).
procedure: Elicit the patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes and compare sides (details shown in the video).
positive: Abnormal (diminished or absent) deep tendon reflex compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: Al Nezari et al. 2013 systematic review/meta-analysis

notes: Weak clinical value but still the best physical-assessment tool available. Companion pages: dermatomes and myotomes lower limb.

title: Straight Leg Raise Test (SLR) for Lumbar Radicular Syndrome
purpose: Tension the sciatic nerve to reproduce lumbar radicular pain, mainly from lumbar disc herniation.
structure: Sciatic nerve and lumbosacral nerve roots (dura). Positive criteria vary in the literature (hip flexion angle versus reproduction of familiar leg pain); no consensus on normative angles. Physiotutors prefer reproduction of familiar leg pain.
procedure: Patient supine. Standing on the affected side, hold the leg so the knee stays fully extended and slowly lift it into hip flexion while observing the patient. Step-wise sensitizers: add ankle dorsiflexion at the point of discomfort, or ask the patient to flex the neck.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar pain shooting down the leg.

accuracy.sensitivity: not reported (described as higher than specificity)
accuracy.source: van der Windt et al. 2010 Cochrane review; Scaia et al. 2012 systematic review (versus surgical findings; most primary studies biased)

notes: No diagnostic value for confirming radicular pain from disc herniation, but at least moderate value for excluding it. Related: crossed SLR (more specific), prone knee bending (L2-L4), bowstring, slump.

title: Crossed Straight Leg Raise Test | Crossed Over Lasègue | Radicular Pain
purpose: Confirm lumbosacral radicular syndrome from intervertebral disc protrusion by raising the uninvolved leg.
structure: Dura and L4-S2 nerve roots pulled caudally; indirect compression of the involved side, especially with large axillary protrusions.
procedure: Patient supine. Flex the uninvolved leg at the hip to about 60-70° with the knee extended.
positive: Shooting pain in the extended (involved) leg along its nerve distribution.

accuracy.source: van der Windt et al. 2010 Cochrane review

notes: Complements the SLR (sensitive, good for exclusion). Related: prone knee bending (L4 and above), bowstring, slump. The illustration mentioned on the page is not in the API text.

title: Bowstring Test | Lumbar Radicular Syndrome
purpose: Evaluate suspected lumbar disc herniation by confirming tension/pressure on the sciatic nerve (also called cram test or posterior tibial nerve sign).
structure: Sciatic/tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa.
procedure: Patient supine. Perform a straight leg raise until symptoms appear, hold the position and flex the knee slightly to about 20° so symptoms ease, then press into the popliteal fossa.
positive: Pressure in the popliteal area reproduces the symptoms/discomfort.

accuracy.specificity: not reported (all 50 patients had herniation, so specificity could not be calculated)

notes: Clinical value unknown. Related: crossed SLR, prone knee bending, SLR, slump.

title: The Slump Test | Neurodynamic Assessment
purpose: Highly provocative dural/neurodynamic test for symptomatic lumbar nerve root compression; different build-ups help distinguish protrusions, epidural adhesions, nerve root compression and intermittent neurogenic claudication.
structure: Dura mater and lumbosacral nerve roots under maximal tension (trunk, neck, knee and ankle components).
procedure: Patient sits on the long edge of the table, hips neutral. Hands behind the back, slump into lumbar and thoracic flexion keeping the head erect; examiner adds overpressure over the shoulders and asks for chin to chest; maintain triple flexion and extend the knee on the affected side (Physiotutors advocate passive extension by the examiner, unlike the video); add passive dorsiflexion. Stop at any stage where symptoms increase.
positive: Reproduction of familiar neurological symptoms. Hamstring tension with limited knee extension or tension at T8/T9 are non-pathological and not positive.

accuracy.source: van der Windt et al. 2010 Cochrane review

notes: Not recommended with suspected severe prolapse/extrusion: lumbar flexion loads the disc and an SLR or standing forward bend usually provokes enough. Even when positive, still do dermatome, myotome and reflex testing. See the Sizer slump build-ups.

title: Prone Knee Bending Test | Reversed Lasègue Test | Femoral Nerve Test
purpose: Tension the femoral nerve to detect lumbar disc herniation with nerve root compression at L2-L4.
structure: Femoral nerve and L2-L4 roots. 90% of radicular syndromes involve L4-L5 or L5-S1; about 5% involve L3-L4, fewer above.
procedure: Patient prone. Carefully flex the knee on the affected side maximally; if flexion beyond 90° is not possible or more femoral nerve stretch is wanted, add passive hip extension. Some authors hold 45-60 s, which may be too provocative in active root compression.
positive: Shooting pain down the leg or anterior thigh on maximal knee flexion, with or without added hip extension (page text says 'hip flexion').
notes: Moderate clinical value to make the diagnosis more likely. Radicular syndrome is usually diagnosed from history alone. Related: SLR, crossed SLR, bowstring, slump.

title: SLR Sizer | Neurodynamic Differential Diagnosis
purpose: Use distal- and proximal-initiation build-ups of the straight leg raise (Sizer et al. 2002) to distinguish primary disc-related disorders (protrusion, prolapse, extrusion with direct root pressure) from secondary disc-related disorders (epidural adhesions, nerve root compression syndrome, intermittent neurogenic claudication).
structure: Dura mater, lumbosacral plexus and sciatic nerve; mobility of the dural sleeve relative to its container.
procedure: Distal initiation: supine; flex hip and knee to slacken the dura; dorsiflex the ankle (distal pre-tension); extend the knee and flex the hip keeping dorsiflexion until symptoms; patient flexes the neck (maximal tension); release dorsiflexion. Proximal initiation: supine; flex hip and knee; patient flexes head and neck (cranial pre-tension); examiner dorsiflexes, extends the knee and flexes the hip until symptoms; patient extends head and neck (dura moves distally).
positive: Primary disc disorder: provocation is maximal at maximal dural tension regardless of direction. Secondary disorder: provocation is direction-specific, maximal with distal initiation, decreasing when neck flexion is added and disappearing when dorsiflexion is released; with proximal initiation pain appears only when head/neck extension releases the proximal pre-tension.
notes: Example mechanism: an irritated root compressed between a degenerative disc bulge and hypertrophic ligamentum flavum hurts more when moved distally through the narrowed path. Related: slump (Sizer), SLR, crossed SLR, prone knee bending.

title: Slump Test Sizer | Neurodynamic Differential Diagnosis
purpose: Use distal- and proximal-initiation build-ups of the slump test (Sizer et al. 2002) to distinguish primary disc-related disorders from dural sleeve adhesions and nerve root compression / intermittent neurogenic claudication.
structure: Dura mater and lumbosacral nerve roots; intervertebral foramen size changes with flexion/extension.
procedure: Start erect, knees 90°, legs off the table. Distal initiation: passive ankle dorsiflexion (distal pre-tension), passive knee extension fixated by the examiner's knee, then chin tuck, neck flexion and trunk slump (maximal tension), then release dorsiflexion. Proximal initiation: full neck flexion and trunk slump first (cranial pre-tension), then dorsiflexion and knee extension, then neck/head extension while staying slumped.
positive: Primary disc disorder: pain rises with tension in either direction (moderate with dorsiflexion + knee extension, maximal with chin tuck/neck flexion, eased by neck extension; proximal: mild with flexion, maximal with added dorsiflexion/knee extension, less with neck extension). Dural sleeve adhesions: pain when the dura moves distally (moderate with distal initiation, less with added neck flexion, none when dorsiflexion is released; proximal: no pain until neck/head extension). Nerve root compression / neurogenic claudication: no pain at all in slump, because lumbar flexion enlarges the foramen.
notes: Same caution as the slump test: avoid with suspected severe prolapse/extrusion. Related: slump, SLR, crossed SLR, prone knee bending.
